A woman in her 30s with a history of right breast cancer, stage IIIa (cT2N2M0). She underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by right modified radical mastectomy and postoperative radiotherapy. vignette:
A 61-year-old woman presented with worsening dyspnea over the previous six months, with acute exacerbation. Symptoms included dyspnea on exertion, 2-pillow orthopnea, fatigue, dry cough, and bilateral lower limb swelling worse in evenings. One episode of lightheadedness occurred a week before presentation. Medical history included a 20-year history of autoimmune condition with joint involvement, complicated by usual interstitial pneumonia pattern interstitial lung disease four years prior and keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Patient had poor therapeutic adherence due to significant barriers to care. Previous surgeries included tonsillectomy and partial hysterectomy. Non-smoker, no alcohol use.

Vital signs: BP 138/86 mmHg, pulse 85/min, temperature 96.5°F (35.8°C), BMI 16.3 kg/m², respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 93% on 3L oxygen. Patient was alert but chronically ill-looking and cachectic. Normal breath sounds on auscultation, no increased work of breathing or accessory muscle use. No jugular venous distention, normal heart sounds. Pupils equal and reactive, no conjunctival injection or scleral icterus. No skin rashes, ulcerations, palpable purpura, or nodules. No palpable lymph nodes. Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended with normal bowel sounds. Muscle tone normal, power 5/5, no cranial nerve deficits. Bilateral ulnar deviation at metacarpophalangeal joints with swan neck deformities at third and fourth fingers bilaterally. No joint swelling, warmth, or redness, but tenderness noted.

vignette:
A 13-year-old girl from a hilly region of Nepal presented with intermittent fever with chills and profuse sweating for 1 month. The fever was low grade, occurring at intervals, and associated with lassitude and dry cough. She had received courses of antibiotics and antipyretics without improvement. She had no travel history to leishmaniasis‐endemic areas. On examination, she appeared pale and ill; temperature was 99.4°F, respiratory rate was increased, and heart rate was elevated. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. There was no icterus, lymphadenopathy, cyanosis, clubbing, edema, or sternal tenderness. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly extending to the umbilical line and mild hepatomegaly, with the liver palpable two fingers below the right midclavicular line. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 5.2 g/dL, total leukocyte count 3150/µL, and absolute neutrophil count 1386/µL. Blood glucose and electrolytes were normal. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 46 mm/h, and C-reactive protein was reactive. Liver enzymes were elevated with ALT 130 U/L and AST 143 U/L. A chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed gross hepatosplenomegaly with a liver span of 16.2 cm and spleen span of 18.1 cm.

vignette:
A 47‐year‐old woman presented with crescendo chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath on exertion for two days. In the emergency department she was hypotensive, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Physical examination showed bilateral fine basal crepitations, a grade 2 decrescendo diastolic murmur, and bilateral pitting lower‐limb edema. She was an active smoker working in warehouse logistics, with no history of substance misuse or family history of cardiovascular disease.

Chest radiography demonstrated congested basal lung fields with mild bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment depressions in the inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed anterior‐wall hypokinesia and moderate‐to‐severe aortic insufficiency; immobile echogenic shadows in the ascending aorta obscured the aortic valve. A computed tomography aortogram excluded aortic dissection. Urgent coronary angiography via the radial approach showed a slit-like left main coronary ostium while the remainder of the coronary arteries was free of atherosclerotic plaque.

These atypical findings prompted investigations for infectious and inflammatory aortitis. Potential causative organisms under consideration included Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella species, Staphylococcus species, and Campylobacter jejuni. Musculoskeletal examination and immunological assays were not suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or Behçet disease.

• Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed a 6×8 mm non-solid structure on the ventricular aspect of the anterior tricuspid leaflet with a “finger-in-glove” blind-ended protrusion, internally empty with filamentous adherent elements (“garland-like”), echogenicity matching adjacent tissue, bulging in systole and relaxing in diastole.  
• The patient remained asymptomatic. Contrast-enhanced chest CT excluded pulmonary embolism, and blood cultures were negative.

vignette:
A 30-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-week history of worsening crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and bloody diarrhea. She denied smoking or alcohol use. Her only medication was a progesterone-only contraceptive, which she had been taking for 2 months.

On examination, her temperature was normal, blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, heart rate 114 bpm, and BMI 32.3. Abdominal palpation revealed diffuse tenderness without guarding or rigidity; bowel sounds were normal.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, metabolic panel, and coagulation studies; C-reactive protein was 4.8 mg/dL. Stool cultures and assays for Clostridioides difficile toxins were negative. Fecal calprotectin was elevated at 2006 µg/g (reference 10–50 µg/g).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated mild thickening of the mid- and distal descending colon with adjacent inflammatory stranding; there was no evidence of perforation, abscess, or diverticulosis.

She was treated with intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and pain medications, and received a single dose of ciprofloxacin and metronidazole. 

Colonoscopy revealed segmental erythema and ulceration in the descending and sigmoid colon, with normal-appearing mucosa in the ascending colon, transverse colon, and rectum. 

Biopsy specimens from the affected segments showed subepithelial edema, hemorrhage, mild crypt architectural distortion, and an acute inflammatory infiltrate without granulomas or dysplasia.

He had frontal bossing, prominent forehead, large open anterior fontanel, micrognathia, high nasal bridge, broad philtrum, short terminal phalanges with bulbous fingertips, and broad, spoon-shaped nails. Laboratory studies showed normal hematologic parameters, serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D level, thyroid function, and insulin-like growth factor 1.

vignette:
A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

vignette:
A 43-year-old man presented with fever, chills, and headache. One month earlier, he had noted a painless ulcer on the prepuce that was healing when he developed fever and fatigue. Ten days before admission, he developed a disseminated maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He reported multiple unprotected sexual contacts over the past three months. He is a man who has sex with men and was diagnosed with HIV infection 10 years ago; he takes abacavir, lamivudine, darunavir, ritonavir, and dolutegravir with an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 1144 cells/μL. One year ago, he was treated with intravenous penicillin G for suspected otosyphilis and had a full clinical and serologic response. 

On examination, he was ill-appearing but not dehydrated. He had painless enlargement of inguinal, axillary, and cervical lymph nodes (up to 3 cm) and a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He had a headache but no nuchal rigidity or Kernig or Brudzinsky signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 63,300/mL with a lymphomonocytic predominance. Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and urine specific gravity were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 19 white cells (95% lymphocytes) with normal glucose and protein concentrations. Blood cultures were repetitively negative.

vignette:
A 60-year-old Ugandan woman, recently diagnosed with HIV and not yet on antiretroviral therapy, was brought to the hospital with a one-day history of reduced consciousness, abrupt onset of aphasia, and urinary incontinence. She also reported a two-day history of dry cough, drenching night sweats, and weight loss but denied fever, headache, neck stiffness, visual disturbances, photophobia, or seizures.

On examination, she appeared wasted (weight 40 kg) and was afebrile (36.6 °C). Vital signs were: blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, pulse 66 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Neurologically, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14/15, with dysarthria but no other focal deficits; neck was supple, and pupils were equal and reactive. Chest and other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Two days before admission, a non-contrast brain CT scan showed multiple enhancing nodular white matter lesions with significant peri-lesional edema and midline shift, as well as several small subcortical non-enhancing hypoattenuating lesions suggestive of infarcts. Initial laboratory testing revealed a CD4 count of 6 cells/mm^3 and a positive serum cryptococcal antigen test with a titer of 1:320. Lumbar puncture was deferred given the CT findings.

vignette:
A 57-year-old man was admitted with a 1-month history of high fever, night sweats, and progressive back pain. He reported touching an unpasteurized sheep stomach with an injured hand about 1 month earlier. Initial outpatient therapy with oral cefprozil provided no lasting benefit. On admission, he had no fever but complained of worsening back pain and malaise.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 7170/mm3 with 80% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 35 mm/hour, a C-reactive protein level of 3.19 mg/dL, and a procalcitonin level of 0.21 ng/mL. A serological test for tuberculosis was negative. He was started on intravenous sulbactam–cefoperazone. On hospital day 6, blood cultures grew a Gram-negative bacillus. That same day, he developed weakness and numbness in both legs and difficulty with urination. Neurologic examination revealed grade 3/5 strength in the right lower limb, grade 4/5 in the left, hypertonia of both lower extremities, and tenderness on percussion and palpation of the T9 and T10 spinous processes.

Contrast-enhanced thoracic magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an inflammatory lesion of the T9 lamina and a posterior epidural abscess compressing the spinal cord at T9–T10. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography showed osteolytic destruction of the neural arch of T9. He was transferred to the Department of Orthopedics for surgical management.

A 68-year-old retired man with no prior medical history presented with two months of dorsal spine pain and gradually progressive motor weakness of the left lower extremity. One week before admission, his weakness acutely worsened, rendering him unable to stand or walk without assistance; there was no history of trauma.  

On neurologic examination, he had spastic paraparesis with weakness of the quadriceps, hamstrings, ankle dorsiflexors, and toe extensors on the left. Patellar and ankle jerks were increased, with sustained clonus at the left ankle and bilateral Babinski signs. The lesion was intermediate in signal intensity on T1-weighted images and homogeneously low in signal on T2-weighted images. On fat-saturated postcontrast T1-weighted images, it demonstrated a thin rim of enhancement with no internal enhancement.

A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a facial angioma. MRI of the brain showed no leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Intraocular pressure measured by Icare tonometry was 22 mm Hg in the right eye and 12 mm Hg in the left. Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Funduscopic examination showed increased retinal vessel tortuosity and a diffusely darker fundus in the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography measured choroidal thickness of 2.2 mm in the right eye versus 1.4 mm in the left. Macular spectral-domain OCT confirmed a thicker choroid in the right eye. Standard automated perimetry detected early visual-field defects in the right eye, and peripapillary OCT showed borderline retinal nerve-fibre-layer thickness on the right. Topical latanoprost was initiated in the right eye, reducing intraocular pressure to 17 mm Hg.

vignette:
A 40-year-old man presented with 5 days of progressive dyspnea. On day 1 he was short of breath only with uphill walking (MMRC grade 1), by day 2 he was breathless on level ground (grade 2), and by day 4 he was dyspneic at rest (grade 4). He also noted central, nonradiating chest pain with coughing, without positional change. He denied fever, night sweats, cyanosis, grunting, palpitations, or hemoptysis. He had three previous hospital admissions, most recently 4 months earlier for acute severe pancreatitis. He had a 5-year history of local alcohol consumption but had abstained for 6 months. 

On examination, pulse was 116/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, temperature 98 °F, and SpO2 95% on 4 L O2 by nasal prong. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees. Chest inspection showed decreased movement on the left; trachea deviated rightward; decreased fremitus and stony dullness over the entire left hemithorax; and absent breath sounds on the left. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, WBC 5530/mm3, CRP 73.9 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L, serum albumin 3.1 g/dL, serum amylase 486 U/L, and lipase 416 U/L. 

Chest radiograph revealed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with tracheal shift to the right, consistent with massive left pleural effusion. 

Ultrasonography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed a large left pleural effusion with passive basal lung collapse, and showed a normal-sized pancreas with heterogeneous echotexture and a small intrapancreatic collection at the tail. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple non-enhancing cystic areas in the pancreas (largest 23×16 mm in the tail), minimal peripancreatic fat stranding, and no main pancreatic duct dilation or parenchymal calcifications. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded 900 mL of dark brown, turbid fluid. Pleural fluid analysis: protein 3.5 g/dL; LDH 1413 U/L; glucose 98 mg/dL; ADA 31.4 U/L; total cell count 100/mm3 (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes); amylase 11,871 U/L; PCV 0.8%; no malignant cells; culture negative; MTB/RIF PCR negative.

A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 57 bpm, first-degree AV block, and a prolonged QTc. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 45–50% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Telemetry captured intermittent high-grade AV block with ventricular escape beats, prompting placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker.

Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries, and left ventriculography showed an LVEF of 35–40%. A permanent dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted, and he was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure.

Outpatient cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 31%, RV ejection fraction of 23%, and mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal anteroseptal wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

vignette:
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

vignette:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

vignette:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

vignette:
A 40-year-old previously healthy man was admitted after 1 week of progressive apathy, unresponsiveness, and immobility. He became bedridden and required a feeding tube and urinary catheter. On transfer, he was in a vegetative state.  
Vital signs: temperature 36.5 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 135/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E3 V1 M3). Pupils 3.5 mm, briskly reactive; corneal reflexes present. Both axial and appendicular muscles were rigid, with flexed arms and extended legs; bilateral Babinski and Chaddock signs were positive.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 3.79×10^9/L, neutrophils 74%, CRP 6.07 mg/L, ESR 21 mm/h; HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ANA, anticardiolipin, ANCA, and T-spot negative. Liver and renal functions were normal.  
Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 50 mmH₂O; CSF clear, protein 3.64 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (blood glucose 5.38 mmol/L), chloride 123 mmol/L, leukocytes 0/mm³. CSF India ink stain and bacterial cultures were negative. CSF oligoclonal bands, AQP4, MOG, and GFAP antibodies were negative; CSF fungal cultures were negative.  
Imaging: Brain CT showed a hypodense lesion in the corpus callosum. MRI revealed a homogeneous mass in the corpus callosum body, hypointense on T1, isointense on T2 FLAIR, with rim enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema on postcontrast T1. vignette:
An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

vignette:
A 74-year-old Spanish-speaking man visiting the United States from Honduras presented with a 2-month history of postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, night sweats, early satiety, and a 10-kg weight loss. One week earlier, an abdominal and pelvic CT scan had shown distal ileitis, and he had received a course of antibiotics without improvement. On re-presentation, he reported worsening symptoms and difficulty tolerating oral intake. He denied hematochezia, diarrhea, or fevers. His medical history was notable for prior appendectomy and recently treated helminth infection.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses, and no evidence of perianal disease. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 35 mg/L, and a fecal calprotectin of 94 μg/mg. Stool studies were negative for enteric pathogens. Repeat CT imaging demonstrated persistent distal ileitis.

Ileocolonoscopy revealed a normal terminal ileum, but a nontraversable distal ileal stricture, cecal ulcers, and patchy loss of vascularity throughout the colon. Segmental biopsies of the ileum and colon were obtained. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was positive. Hepatitis B serologies showed a reactive core total antibody, a reactive e antigen, negative surface antigen, and undetectable HBV DNA. He was started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis.

vignette:
A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 2-month history of intermittent painless hematuria with passage of clots. She denied dysuria, frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms, and there was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs and abdominal and pelvic exams were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL requiring blood transfusion; serum creatinine and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 2.9 × 2.5 × 2.4 cm polypoidal mass arising from the posterolateral wall of the bladder dome; both kidneys and the upper tracts appeared normal. Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

vignette:
A 17-year-old single Turkish woman presented with a 3-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. She had no known exposure to tuberculosis. On examination she was afebrile with tender right lower abdominal quadrant and no rebound. While under observation, a second abdominopelvic ultrasound was interpreted as suggestive of retrocecal appendicitis. The patient was taken to the operating room via a McBurney’s incision. A 15 × 6 cm cystic mass with regular margins was found arising from the right tubo-ovarian complex; the appendix appeared clinically normal. The mass was excised intact, the tubo-ovarian structures were preserved, and on incision of the cyst wall purulent fluid was noted. Cultures were deferred until after the weekend.

A 36-year-old woman with a 17-year history of migraine headaches was referred for management of a right-sided migraine characterized by a visual aura of gray-white spots followed by pain behind the right eye radiating to the right frontal, temporal, and suboccipital regions. In January 2023, she developed a right orbital and medial cheek headache radiating to the right lateral jaw, ear, and down the right suboccipital region. Treatment with ketorolac, rizatriptan, and a 7-day dexamethasone taper failed to resolve her symptoms. She then received naratriptan, prochlorperazine, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and diphenhydramine without improvement. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable. Given refractory symptoms, she underwent an ultrasound-guided right sphenopalatine ganglion block with 4 mL of bupivacaine 0.25% and 1 mL of dexamethasone 4 mg/mL. This treatment also failed to resolve her symptoms.

Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

A 67-year-old woman with a 4-day history of fever and cough was admitted to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR. Five days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, prompting intubation and transfer to the ICU. Her comorbidities included diabetes mellitus with dialysis-dependent nephropathy, angina, prior gastric cancer resection, and spinal‐canal stenosis; she was on an antiplatelet agent.  
On arrival: temperature 34 °C; blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; heart rate 102 beats/min; GCS E1VtM1 under deep sedation. Arterial blood gas (on pressure‐control ventilation: PEEP 8 cmH₂O, PiP 25 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.5) showed pH 7.309, PaCO₂ 41.5 mmHg, PaO₂ 78.2 mmHg.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 13,900/µL; CRP 13.1 mg/dL; D-dimer 7.25 µg/mL; APTT 170 s; INR 1.35.  
Chest CT: bilateral ground‐glass opacities with lower-lung predominance. Abdominal CT: no overt abnormalities or thromboembolism, but diffuse edema of the intestine, including the transverse colon, and marked sclerotic changes in abdominal vessels.  
She continued dexamethasone (6 mg/day) and commenced continuous renal replacement therapy. On ICU day 3, cefepime was started for ventilator-associated pneumonia. The APTT fell to 51.5 s, and prophylactic-dose unfractionated heparin was initiated to target an APTT of ~60 s.
